items.prompt: Define opportunity cost.
items.canonical_answer: The opportunity cost of a choice is the next-best alternative given up when that choice is made.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must name the next-best alternative given up. An example alone is not a definition.

items.prompt: A school in Opuwo has N$20 000 spare and must choose between a water tank and a set of textbooks. Explain why the school's choice involves an opportunity cost.
items.canonical_answer: The money is scarce: the same N$20 000 cannot buy both the tank and the books. Because resources are limited, choosing the water tank means the textbooks, the next-best alternative, are given up. The value of the lost textbooks is the opportunity cost of the tank.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for identifying that the scarce money forces a choice, because one purchase excludes the other. Second reason: award for naming the textbooks as the next-best alternative given up - the opportunity cost.

items.prompt: Explain the features that tell a need apart from a want.
items.canonical_answer: A need is required for survival - food, water, shelter, basic clothing - while a want is something a person would like but can live without. The features that separate them are: survival depends on a need, whereas a want improves life without being essential; and wants are effectively unlimited, while the needs a person must meet are a much shorter list. Both are satisfied by goods and services.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element stated - survival versus preference, and unlimited wants against a short list of needs - and one mark for developing each with an example of what it includes.

items.prompt: Define specialisation.
items.canonical_answer: Specialisation is when a worker, a business or a country concentrates on producing a limited range of goods or services instead of trying to produce everything for itself.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include concentration on a limited range of output. Naming only one worker-level example is not a definition.

items.prompt: A Tsumeb juice bottler has moved each worker onto a single stage of the line. Explain how this change could lead to more output a day, and how it could also lead to problems for the business.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: if each worker stays on one narrow stage, practice builds speed and skill, so each stage is completed faster and with fewer mistakes. Mechanism: faster stages mean the line produces more bottles each day, and the cost of producing each bottle tends to fall, so the business can price more competitively and win sales. Consequence for the business: higher output and a better chance of survival and profit. But the same narrowness can bore workers, so motivation and output can fall, and if the one specialist on a stage is absent the whole line may stop.
marking_guidance: Condition: the mechanism must be tied to the given starting point of one stage per worker. Mechanism: award for the why or how - practice builds speed, so output rises. Consequence: award for the effect on the business - unit cost and competitiveness - and a second consequence for the stakeholder risk of bored workers or a stalled line.

items.prompt: Oshakati Fruit Processors moved its 24 workers from whole-shift bottling to a line where each does one step, and output rose from 400 to 560 bottles a day. Two of the most experienced workers have asked to return to their old varied jobs. Explain what the figures suggest about specialisation here, and what the manager should weigh before deciding on the two requests.
items.canonical_answer: The context figures show the specialisation gain: 560 bottles a day against 400 before, so each worker now averages 23 bottles a day against about 17 before. The reasoning is that concentrating on one step built speed, which is where the extra 160 bottles a day came from. But the two requests signal the cost side: experienced workers can find narrow repetition demotivating, and demotivated specialists may leave, taking their skill with them. Conclusion: the manager should weigh the retention of skilled people against the higher output before refusing or granting the requests - perhaps by rotating the two workers between stages, keeping much of the gain while answering the complaint.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the named business's facts - 560 against 400 bottles, 24 workers. Reasoning: award for the link between specialisation and the output rise, and between repetition and the requests to leave. Conclusion: award a judgement for this business that follows the reasoning, such as rotation.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the division of labour as a way of organising production.
items.canonical_answer: The division of labour breaks one product's work into narrow stages and gives each worker a single stage. Its features are: each worker repeats one task, so practice builds speed and skill; output per worker rises as a result; and the arrangement has built-in weaknesses, because the work can become repetitive and demotivating and the line depends on every specialist being present. It is a specific form of specialisation applied to the stages of one product rather than a separate idea.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - one narrow stage per worker, speed and skill from repetition, rising output - and for what it includes on the cost side: repetition demotivates and absence stalls the line.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Specialisation and the division of labour are two names for the same thing." Explain why this is wrong.
items.canonical_answer: The error is treating the broader idea and one specific form of it as identical. Specialisation is any concentration on a limited range of output, whether by a worker, a business or a whole country; the division of labour is one particular arrangement, in which the stages of one product are split between workers, each doing a single stage. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the statement concerns the range of things produced, which is specialisation, or the sharing of one product's stages between workers, which is the division of labour. A lamb farmer who specialises in meat is not practising the division of labour, because no product stages are being shared out.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact the two ideas differ in scope - any concentration on a limited range versus stage-sharing on one product. Award the second mark for the test that separates the confused pair.

items.prompt: Define the purpose of business activity.
items.canonical_answer: The purpose of business activity is to organise scarce resources to produce the goods and services that satisfy people's needs and wants, and to exchange that output for money.

items.prompt: Explain why people in an economy can consume more goods and services than they could make for themselves.
items.canonical_answer: Each person specialises in a narrow line of work and exchanges the output for money, which buys everything else. The joiner, the farmer and the nurse each produce more of their own product than they need because concentrating on one kind of work builds skill, and through trade each obtains the others' products. Self-sufficiency would force every person to produce everything at a low standard of skill, so specialisation followed by exchange is the reason consumption runs far beyond what any individual could make alone.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for specialised production raising each person's output, because concentration builds skill. Second reason: award for exchange - trade turns one specialised output into many products, which is why consumption exceeds self-production.

items.prompt: Explain the main elements of the purpose of business activity.
items.canonical_answer: The main elements are: identifying what people need or want; organising the scarce resources - land, labour, capital and enterprise - to produce it; exchanging the output for money; and, in doing so, creating jobs and wages for workers while the owners aim to make a profit. What it includes above all is the transformation of scarce resources into satisfaction, because no one can make everything they want for themselves.
marking_guidance: Elements: award one mark for each part - identifying wants, organising scarce resources, exchange for money - and one mark for what the purpose includes for people: jobs, wages and the owners' profit aim.

items.prompt: Define added value.
items.canonical_answer: Added value is the difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials and other inputs used to make it.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must relate the gap to selling price minus bought-in input costs. A formula such as "what is left for the business" is not precise enough.

items.prompt: Explain how a business benefits from adding value rather than simply reselling what it buys in.
items.canonical_answer: A reseller passes on a product unchanged and earns only the small gap between the buying price and the selling price. A business that transforms its inputs creates a bigger gap, because the finished product is worth more to customers than the raw materials were. That larger gap is what funds wages, rent and every other running cost, so the business is more likely to cover them and still leave a profit. A higher added value also gives the business room to cut prices or spend on marketing if competition arrives, which leads to a stronger position than a reseller's thin margin allows.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for the gap being larger after transformation, developed with the reason that customers pay more for finished goods, and developed further to the consequence that the gap funds running costs and so leads to a better chance of profit and pricing room.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of using added value as evidence that a business is doing well.
items.canonical_answer: A high added value only shows that the gap between selling price and bought-in inputs is wide. It says nothing about the business's other costs: if wages, rent, transport and marketing are heavy, they can swallow the whole gap, so the business makes a loss even while its added value looks strong. Judging success on added value alone can therefore flatter a business whose profit is negative.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for the gap ignoring other costs, developed because wages, rent and transport must be paid out of it, which leads to the consequence that a business can show high added value and still fail.

items.prompt: Kavango Woodworks buys timber, glue and varnish for N$220 per chair and sells each chair for N$580. It is considering a design upgrade that would raise input costs to N$260 a chair and, the owner believes, raise the price customers accept to N$680. Explain what happens to Kavango Woodworks' added value per chair under the upgrade, and what the owner should check before going ahead.
items.canonical_answer: Now the gap is N$580 less N$220, giving N$360 a chair. After the upgrade it would be N$680 less N$260, giving N$420 a chair, so the facts here suggest added value rises by N$60 per chair. The reasoning is that the design upgrade raises what customers are willing to pay by more than it raises input costs. The owner should check the assumption behind the N$680: provided customers really accept the higher price, added value rises; if the upgrade fails to lift the price, the added value falls to N$320 and the upgrade has made the position worse.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using this business's facts - N$360 against N$420 per chair from the figures given. Reasoning: award for the link between the design upgrade and what customers accept. Conclusion: award a choice for the upgrade conditional on the price assumption holding.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the main ways a business can increase its added value.
items.canonical_answer: The main ways come in two parts. On the price side: improving quality, building a brand customers trust, better design, greater convenience such as delivery, and service around the sale - each raises what customers are willing to pay. On the cost side: negotiating cheaper bought-in materials and cutting material waste - each lowers the input cost. What the two parts include is the same arithmetic: added value is the gap between the two, so widening the gap from either side increases it, provided the selling price is not cut by as much as the input saving.
marking_guidance: Features: award for the elements of the price route - quality, brand, design, convenience, service - and for the cost route as what it includes: cheaper inputs and less waste, with the condition that the price is not cut to match.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Omuthitu Potters added N$140 of value to each pot, so its profit must be N$140 a pot." Explain why this reasoning is wrong.
items.canonical_answer: The mistake is subtracting only the bought-in inputs and calling the rest profit. In fact, added value of N$140 is the gap between the N$180 selling price and the N$40 of clay, glaze and firewood; before any profit appears, the potters' wages, workshop rent, transport and every other running cost must also be paid out of that gap. The test that tells the two ideas apart: ask which costs have been taken away. Added value takes away only bought-in inputs; profit is what remains after every cost of the business is paid, so it is a smaller figure - and can be negative where added value is large.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact only input costs were subtracted, wrongly treating the rest as profit. Award the second mark for the test that separates the measures - which costs were taken away before the figure.

items.prompt: The manager of a small Windhoek print shop is deciding whether to keep three general assistants who each do every job, or to reorganise so one handles design, one printing and one finishing. Write several linked points for the manager: state two advantages and two disadvantages of the reorganisation, each with a reason, and close with your choice for this business.
items.canonical_answer: Advantages: each assistant practises one stage, so speed and quality at that stage tend to rise, which lifts the shop's daily output; and work flows in a predictable sequence, so delivery promises are easier to keep. Disadvantages: repetitive work can demotivate assistants, who may leave and take their specialist skill with them; and if the one specialist on a stage is absent, that stage stalls the whole job. Choice for this business: with only three assistants the risks bite harder than in a large firm, so a middle path - specialise, but train every assistant to cover a second stage - keeps the output gain while limiting the single-point-of-failure risk.
marking_guidance: Point: award for each point stated, up to two per side. Reason: award for the because behind each point - practice builds speed, repetition demotivates. Context: award for applying each point to the three-assistant print shop rather than in the abstract.

items.prompt: Okahandja Leather Works makes school shoes. Bought-in leather and other materials cost N$60 a pair and the shop sells a pair for N$150. A national chain store offers to take 2 000 pairs a year at N$120 a pair if the design is upgraded at an extra N$8 of materials a pair. Using the figures, consider whether the workshop should accept the offer.
items.canonical_answer: The figures: added value now is N$150 less N$60, giving N$90 a pair. On the chain store contract it would be N$120 less N$68, giving N$52 a pair, so added value per pair falls by N$38. Judged on total added value the contract is worth 2 000 pairs at N$52, giving N$104 000 a year, against which the workshop keeps its N$90 margin on every pair it sells at full price - it would take about 1 156 such pairs to match N$104 000. The decisive criterion is therefore volume: the contract pays a thinner margin but on a guaranteed 2 000 pairs. The counterargument is that the chain store's customers may be the same ones paying N$150 today, in which case each switched sale loses the workshop N$38 of added value; the 2 000 pairs have an opportunity cost, because the capacity used for them is then not serving full-price customers, and the recommendation depends on that check. Recommendation: accept, provided the contract pairs are extra sales rather than replacements for full-price sales and the workshop can supply 2 000 pairs without overtime costs eating the margin.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on the contract. Context: award for using the figures - N$90 against N$52 a pair and the N$104 000 total. Criterion: award for naming what decides it, volume of guaranteed sales against margin per pair. Counterargument: award for the risk that contract sales replace full-price sales, which counts against accepting. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on the replacement check and capacity costs.

items.prompt: Plan, without writing the full answer, a response to this 12-mark task: "A business that increases its added value will be more successful." Consider this view. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the case against your judgement, and the conditions the final recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, define the terms: added value as the gap between selling price and bought-in input costs; success for a business measured against its objective, usually profit. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: a wider gap funds wages, rent and marketing, so the business is more likely to cover all costs and profit remains - success supported. Paragraph 3, the case against: added value ignores the other costs and the customer's willingness to pay at all - an upgrade that raises input costs faster than the accepted price reduces the gap, so the drive to increase added value can make a business less successful if the market rejects the higher price; there is also an opportunity cost, because money spent on raising the gap cannot be spent elsewhere. Paragraph 4, judgement: the view holds where the price rise is accepted and the input saving is not passed on in a lower price; the criterion is whether total added value rises without reducing sales volume. Recommendation conditional on: the market accepting the price, and the business's other costs staying within the widened gap.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the plan must state the verdict the answer would reach. Context: the plan must use facts about how added value is built - price acceptance and input costs. Criterion: the plan must name what decides the verdict, total added value against volume. Counterargument: the plan must include the case against the view. Condition: the recommendation must depend on stated conditions - price acceptance and other costs.

items.prompt: Rundu Riverside Juices is a two-year-old business with six staff. Each worker currently prepares, bottles and packs fruit juice, and the owner is proud that "no one here is just a cog". Output is 250 bottles a day and buyers comment that the bottles look inconsistent. A supermarket buyer has offered a trial order if the look becomes uniform and the price drops by 10 per cent. Analyse the situation and recommend what the owner should do.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the inconsistencies point to a lack of stage-by-stage specialisation - when every worker does every stage, no one builds the settled routine that makes bottles uniform, so practice never builds the speed or consistency the buyer wants. A division of labour - one worker on preparation, one on bottling, one on packing, with cover trained - would tend to raise output above 250 bottles a day and make the look uniform, giving the business its chance at the supermarket trial. The 10 per cent price cut narrows the gap between price and input cost, so part of the extra value created by the higher output would be handed to the buyer as the price concession; whether the total added value still rises depends on how far output grows and whether material waste falls as the routine settles. Recommendation: introduce the specialised stages with cross-training so no single absence stalls the line, and accept the trial order provided the expected output rise holds the total added value up despite the lower price per bottle. The judgement is a close one because the owner's staff culture values variety, so the change should be introduced with the workers' agreement - rotation between stages can keep both.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on the specialised stages and the trial. Context: award for using the facts of the business - six staff, 250 bottles, inconsistent bottles, the 10 per cent price cut. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - uniformity and total added value against the price concession. Counterargument: award for the case against the change - the culture risk and the thinner margin. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on output growth and staff agreement.
